angle: Do explanations actually help the humans who use them? User studies, SOC-analyst studies, human-grounded evaluation, and the runtime cost of producing explanations (matters at line rate for networking).
retrieval_note: Built from arXiv API (6 queries), DBLP API, and targeted WebSearch confirmations on 2026-08-21. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned HTTP 429 (rate-limited) for the whole session; every entry below was verified against at least one actually-retrieved source (arXiv Atom feed, DBLP JSON, or a search-result page). Citation counts are 0 unless a retrieved source stated one.

papers.title: 99% False Positives: A Qualitative Study of SOC Analysts' Perspectives on Security Alarms
papers.authors: Bushra A. Alahmadi, Louise Axon, Ivan Martinovic
papers.relevance: Survey (N=20) plus qualitative study (N=21) of SOC practitioners showing most 'false positives' are benign triggers and that alarms must be Reliable, Explainable, Analytical, Contextual, Transferable -- the canonical statement of what analysts actually need from explanation-bearing alerts.

papers.title: Matched and Mismatched SOCs: A Qualitative Study on Security Operations Center Issues
papers.authors: Faris Bugra Kokulu, Ananta Soneji, Tiffany Bao, Yan Shoshitaishvili, Ziming Zhao, Adam Doupé, Gail-Joon Ahn
papers.relevance: 18 semi-structured interviews with SOC analysts and managers revealing manager/analyst disagreements (including about tool automation and visibility) that any XAI-for-SOC deployment must survive; grounds the 'who is the explanation for' question.

papers.title: Turning Contradictions into Innovations or: How We Learned to Stop Whining and Improve Security Operations
papers.authors: Sathya Chandran Sundaramurthy, John McHugh, Xinming Ou, Michael Wesch, Alexandru G. Bardas, S. Raj Rajagopalan
papers.relevance: 3.5 years of anthropological fieldwork with students embedded as analysts in three SOCs; shows unresolved operational contradictions cause burnout and tool rejection -- context for why analyst-facing explanations succeed or fail.

papers.title: A Human Capital Model for Mitigating Security Analyst Burnout
papers.authors: Sathya Chandran Sundaramurthy, Alexandru G. Bardas, Jacob Case, Xinming Ou, Michael Wesch, John McHugh, S. Raj Rajagopalan
papers.relevance: Ethnography-derived model of analyst burnout as cyclic interaction of human, technical, and managerial factors; motivates workload-reducing (not just transparency-adding) uses of XAI in SOCs.

papers.title: An Assessment of the Usability of Machine Learning Based Tools for the Security Operations Center
papers.authors: Sean Oesch, Robert Bridges, Jared Smith, Justin Beaver, John Goodall, Kelly Huffer, Craig Miles, Dan Scofield
papers.relevance: First in-situ usability study of ML-based detection tools inside operational (Naval) SOCs; documents serious interface violations and analyst mistrust of ML outputs -- direct evidence on whether ML/XAI tooling helps real analysts.

papers.title: Explainable AI in Cybersecurity Operations: Lessons Learned from xAI Tool Deployment
papers.authors: Megan Nyre-Yu, Elizabeth S. Morris, Blake Moss, Charles Smutz, Michael R. Smith
papers.relevance: Deployment study of two xAI prototypes with working cyber analysts (Sandia); reports that lack of trust/transparency drives hesitation and distills lessons on fitting explanations into operational workflows -- one of very few real xAI-in-SOC field studies.

papers.title: Considerations for Deploying xAI Tools in the Wild: Lessons Learned from xAI Deployment in a Cybersecurity Operations Setting
papers.authors: Megan Nyre-Yu, Michael R. Smith, et al.
papers.relevance: Companion workshop paper to the USEC study; practical considerations (integration, analyst time budgets, explanation consumption) for deploying xAI tools in operational security settings.

papers.title: The Challenge of Detecting Sophisticated Attacks: Insights from SOC Analysts
papers.authors: Olusola Akinrolabu, Ioannis Agrafiotis, Arnau Erola
papers.relevance: Interview-based study of SOC analysts on detecting sophisticated attacks; early evidence of the tooling/insight gaps that analyst-facing explanation systems claim to fill.

papers.title: Assessing a Decision Support Tool for SOC Analysts
papers.authors: Jassim Happa, Ioannis Agrafiotis, Martin Helmhout, Thomas Bashford-Rogers, Michael Goldsmith, Sadie Creese
papers.venue: ACM Digital Threats: Research and Practice (DTRAP)
papers.relevance: Human evaluation of a decision-support/visualization tool with SOC analysts -- a template for measuring whether added machine reasoning actually improves analyst judgments rather than assuming it.

papers.title: Evaluating Explanation Methods for Deep Learning in Security
papers.authors: Alexander Warnecke, Daniel Arp, Christian Wressnegger, Konrad Rieck
papers.relevance: THE evaluation framework for XAI in security: adds security-specific criteria -- completeness, stability, robustness, and crucially EFFICIENCY (runtime) -- and shows black-box perturbation methods (LIME/KernelSHAP-style) are orders of magnitude slower than white-box gradient methods across security systems including network intrusion detection.

papers.title: SoK: Explainable Machine Learning for Computer Security Applications
papers.authors: Azqa Nadeem, Daniël Vos, Clinton Cao, Luca Pajola, Simon Dieck, Robert Baumgartner, Sicco Verwer
papers.relevance: Systematizes 300+ security-XAI papers by stakeholder and objective; headline finding for this angle: 'user studies for explanation evaluation are conducted in only 14% of the cases' -- quantifies the human-evaluation gap in security XAI.

papers.title: AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes (Trustee)
papers.authors: Arthur S. Jacobs, Roman Beltiukov, Walter Willinger, Ronaldo A. Ferreira, Arpit Gupta, Lisandro Z. Granville
papers.relevance: Trustee extracts high-fidelity, low-complexity decision-tree explanations plus a 'trust report' from black-box network-security models so practitioners can spot shortcut learning, spurious correlations, and o.o.d. fragility -- global explanation aimed squarely at network operators' trust decisions.

papers.title: DeepAID: Interpreting and Improving Deep Learning-based Anomaly Detection in Security Applications
papers.authors: Dongqi Han, Zhiliang Wang, Wenqi Chen, Ying Zhong, Su Wang, Han Zhang, Jiahai Yang, Xingang Shi, Xia Yin
papers.relevance: Interpretation framework for unsupervised security anomaly detectors (incl. Kitsune network IDS) built around operator tasks -- understanding decisions, diagnosing mistakes, reducing FPs -- with security-domain constraints and efficiency evaluated; bridges explanation quality and operational usefulness.

papers.title: Interpreting Deep Learning-Based Networking Systems (Metis)
papers.authors: Zili Meng, Minhu Wang, Jiasong Bai, Mingwei Xu, Hongzi Mao, Hongxin Hu
papers.relevance: Converts DNN policies in networking systems into decision trees / hypergraph highlights so network operators can design, debug, deploy, and adjust them; the networking community's own argument that uninterpretability blocks deployment.

papers.title: LEMNA: Explaining Deep Learning based Security Applications
papers.authors: Wenbo Guo, Dongliang Mu, Jun Xu, Purui Su, Gang Wang, Xinyu Xing
papers.relevance: Security-specific local explanation method (fused-lasso + mixture regression) built because LIME/SHAP assumptions fail on security models (RNNs, feature dependency); the standard baseline that later human/runtime evaluations (e.g., Warnecke) test.

papers.title: DeepCASE: Semi-Supervised Contextual Analysis of Security Events
papers.authors: Thijs van Ede, Hojjat Aghakhani, Noah Spahn, Riccardo Bortolameotti, Marco Cova, Andrea Continella, Maarten van Steen, Andreas Peter, Christopher Kruegel, Giovanni Vigna
papers.relevance: Interpretable (attention-based) contextual clustering of security event sequences explicitly designed to cut security operators' manual inspection workload by ~95%; operationalizes 'helping the human' as workload reduction with operator-set policies.

papers.title: On the Effect of Ruleset Tuning and Data Imbalance on Explainable Network Security Alert Classifications: a Case-Study on DeepCASE
papers.authors: Koen T. W. Teuwen, Sam Baggen, Emmanuele Zambon, Luca Allodi
papers.relevance: Shows SOC label imbalance and detection-rule tuning materially change both performance AND the correctness of the explanations DeepCASE-style systems give analysts -- explanation quality is an operational variable, not a fixed property.

papers.title: Evaluating explainable AI for deep learning-based network intrusion detection system alert classification
papers.authors: Rajesh Kalakoti, Risto Vaarandi, Hayretdin Bahsi
papers.venue: arXiv (journal version of TalTech SOC study)
papers.relevance: LSTM alert-prioritization on real NIDS alerts from the TalTech SOC; compares LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT on faithfulness/complexity/robustness/reliability AND validates the selected features with the SOC's own analysts -- rare end-to-end XAI-for-NIDS evaluation with practitioner grounding.

papers.title: Explaining Intrusion Alert Decisions of Deep Learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems for Security Analysts
papers.authors: Ayush Kumar, Vrizlynn L. L. Thing
papers.relevance: EXP-SEC translates raw feature attributions from DL-based NIDS into domain-level explanations (suspect-packet isolation, SOC-aligned multi-stage mapping) on the argument that feature-importance lists are not consumable by analysts as-is.

papers.title: SoK: Pragmatic Assessment of Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Giovanni Apruzzese, Pavel Laskov, Johannes Schneider
papers.relevance: Defines 'pragmatic assessment' of ML-NIDS (hundreds of configs, four hardware platforms, runtime/cost reporting) and validates the notion with a user study of security practitioners -- the practitioner-skepticism framing this whole sub-literature answers.

papers.title: E-XAI: Evaluating Black-Box Explainable AI Frameworks for Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Osvaldo Arreche, Tanish R. Guntur, Jack W. Roberts, Mustafa Abdallah
papers.relevance: End-to-end benchmark of SHAP and LIME over multiple black-box NIDS models with six metrics that explicitly include computational efficiency/runtime alongside descriptive accuracy, sparsity, stability, robustness -- the NIDS instantiation of Warnecke-style evaluation.

papers.title: A Lightweight, Efficient and Explainable-by-Design Convolutional Neural Network for Internet Traffic Classification (LEXNet)
papers.authors: Kevin Fauvel, Fuxing Chen, Dario Rossi
papers.relevance: Traffic-classification CNN with a prototype layer giving explanations BY DESIGN while staying lightweight enough for resource-constrained networking hardware -- the 'avoid post-hoc explanation cost entirely' answer to line-rate explainability.

papers.title: EXPLORA: AI/ML EXPLainability for the Open RAN
papers.authors: Claudio Fiandrino, Leonardo Bonati, Salvatore D'Oro, Michele Polese, Tommaso Melodia, Joerg Widmer
papers.relevance: Explains DRL agents controlling the Open RAN via attributed action-graphs, deployed on an O-RAN-compliant testbed (Colosseum) and designed for real-time operation inside RAN control loops -- concrete evidence on explanation latency budgets in production-like networks.

papers.title: Feature Attribution in 5G Intrusion Detection: A Statistical vs. Logic-Based Comparison
papers.authors: Federica Uccello, Simin Nadjm-Tehrani

papers.title: TRUST XAI: Model-Agnostic Explanations for AI With a Case Study on IIoT Security

papers.relevance: Statistical model-agnostic explainer (factor analysis + mutual information + Gaussian likelihoods) benchmarked on IIoT/network security data; explicitly positions itself as superior to LIME in performance AND speed, targeting online explanation of new samples.

papers.title: Human-Centered Explainability in AI-Enhanced UI Security Interfaces
papers.authors: Mona Rajhans
papers.relevance: Controlled user study with security practitioners comparing explanation styles (natural language, confidence visualizations, counterfactuals) in security dashboards; explanation style significantly shifts trust calibration, decision accuracy, and cognitive load.

papers.relevance: Simulation study (LR/RF on UNSW-NB15) showing misaligned confidence/uncertainty displays amplify costly triage errors; a decision-theoretic account of trust signals -- but no human subjects, so its interface claims await user-study validation.

papers.title: That Escalated Quickly: An ML Framework for Alert Prioritization

papers.relevance: Production alert-prioritization system measured in analyst-relevant units (22.9% faster response, 54% FP suppression); the workload-metrics counterpoint to explanation-centric help for SOC humans.

papers.authors: Amin Nayebi, Sindhu Tipirneni, Chandan K. Reddy, Brandon Foreman, Vignesh Subbian

papers.authors: Chenghao Yang, Fan Yin, He He, Kai-Wei Chang, Xiaofei Ma, Bing Xiang

papers.authors: Zana Buçinca, Phoebe Lin, Krzysztof Z. Gajos, Elena L. Glassman

papers.authors: Forough Poursabzi-Sangdeh, Daniel G. Goldstein, Jake M. Hofman, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Hanna Wallach

papers.authors: Harmanpreet Kaur, Harsha Nori, Samuel Jenkins, Rich Caruana, Hanna Wallach, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan
papers.relevance: Contextual inquiry (N=11) + survey (N=197): data scientists over-trust and misuse GAM/SHAP tooling and often cannot describe the visualizations -- practitioners misreading the very tools SOCs are told to adopt.

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning in Deployment
papers.authors: Umang Bhatt, Alice Xiang, Shubham Sharma, Adrian Weller, Ankur Taly, Yunhan Jia, Joydeep Ghosh, Ruchir Puri, José M. F. Moura, Peter Eckersley
papers.relevance: ~50 interviews across ~30 organizations: deployed explainability overwhelmingly serves ML engineers for debugging, not end users -- the deployment-reality check for claims that XAI serves analysts.

papers.title: Questioning the AI: Informing Design Practices for Explainable AI User Experiences
papers.authors: Q. Vera Liao, Daniel Gruen, Sarah Miller
papers.relevance: Interviews with 20 practitioners yielding the XAI Question Bank (what users actually ask of AI) -- a requirements-elicitation method transferable to asking what SOC analysts need from a traffic classifier's explanations.

papers.authors: Q. Vera Liao, Kush R. Varshney
papers.relevance: Survey bridging XAI algorithms and HCI evaluation practice; frames explainability as an inherently human-centric property to be validated with users, not benchmarks.

papers.title: In Search of Verifiability: Explanations Rarely Enable Complementary Performance in AI-Advised Decision Making
papers.authors: Raymond Fok, Daniel S. Weld
papers.relevance: Synthesis arguing explanations only help when they let the human VERIFY the answer, and most tasks don't afford verification -- predicts exactly when NIDS-alert explanations will and won't improve triage decisions.

papers.title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
papers.authors: Helena Vasconcelos, Matthew Jörke, Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin, Tobias Gerstenberg, Michael S. Bernstein, Ranjay Krishna
papers.relevance: Five studies showing people strategically engage with explanations based on cost-benefit: explanations reduce overreliance when they cut verification effort enough -- a mechanism directly applicable to time-pressured alert triage.

papers.authors: Yunfeng Zhang, Q. Vera Liao, Rachel K. E. Bellamy

papers.authors: Jasper van der Waa, Elisabeth Nieuwburg, Anita Cremers, Mark Neerincx

papers.title: Use-Case-Grounded Simulations for Explanation Evaluation (SimEvals)
papers.authors: Valerie Chen, Nari Johnson, Nicholay Topin, Gregory Plumb, Ameet Talwalkar
papers.relevance: Trains agents to screen which explanation methods are worth an expensive human study -- a practical answer to the cost of running SOC-analyst experiments.

papers.authors: Ahmed Alqaraawi, Martin Schuessler, Philipp Weiß, Enrico Costanza, Nadia Berthouze
papers.relevance: Between-subjects study: saliency maps gave 'very limited help' in predicting classifier behavior on new inputs -- cautionary for saliency-over-packet-bytes visualizations popular in DL traffic classification.

papers.authors: Leon Sixt, Martin Schuessler, Oana-Iuliana Popescu, Philipp Weiß, Tim Landgraf
papers.relevance: N=240 study where a simple baseline (showing example outputs) beat concept-based explanations for bias discovery -- benchmark discipline for claims that sophisticated explanations help users.

papers.title: What Makes for a Good Saliency Map? A User Study
papers.authors: Leon Kares, Timo Speith, et al.
papers.relevance: N=166 between-subjects comparison of LIME/Grad-CAM/Guided Backprop finding subjective and objective measures disagree and mathematical saliency metrics are often counterintuitive to humans.

papers.title: Does Explanation Correctness Matter? Linking Computational XAI Evaluation to Human Understanding
papers.authors: Gregor Baer, Chao Zhang, Isel Grau, Pieter Van Gorp
papers.relevance: N=200 study manipulating attribution correctness in time-series classification: correctness affects human understanding non-linearly and 'not all differences in functional correctness translate to differences in human understanding' -- links the benchmark world to the human world.

papers.title: Explaining Network Intrusion Detection System Using Explainable AI Framework
papers.authors: Shraddha Mane, Dattaraj Rao
papers.relevance: Early NIDS-XAI pipeline layering SHAP, LIME, Contrastive Explanations, ProtoDash and Boolean rules over a DNN on NSL-KDD; representative of the analyst-facing-in-name-only genre that later human studies interrogate.

papers.title: Building Transparency in Deep Learning-Powered Network Traffic Classification: A Traffic-Explainer Framework
papers.authors: Riya Ponraj, Ram Durairajan, Yu Wang
papers.relevance: Model-agnostic perturbation-based explainer purpose-built for traffic classification (claims ~42% improvement over generic explanation methods on application classification and traffic-localization tasks); no human study, but the NTC-native explanation baseline.

notes: SOURCES USED: arXiv API (6+ queries), DBLP API (uni-trier mirror; dblp.org reset connections), 12+ targeted WebSearches; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs 429-rate-limited the entire session (OpenAlex Retry-After ~4h), so citation counts are mostly unavailable (0 = unknown). RECURRING DATASETS: NSL-KDD and UNSW-NB15 dominate NIDS-XAI benchmarks (E-XAI, Mane, Chowdhury); CICIDS-family implied in several; real operational data is rare but growing -- TalTech SOC alerts (Kalakoti), Lastline/commercial event streams (DeepCASE), Microsoft GUIDE (~1M analyst-annotated incidents), Naval SOCs in-situ (Oesch), Sandia operational deployment (Nyre-Yu), O-RAN Colosseum testbed (EXPLORA). RECURRING EXPLANATION METHODS: SHAP is hegemonic (KernelSHAP/TreeSHAP and a whole cottage industry of accelerations: FastSHAP, GPUTreeShap, Fast TreeSHAP, SHEAR, WindowSHAP, amortized text-Shapley); then LIME, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, LRP; security-native methods: LEMNA (mixture regression), DeepAID (constrained optimization for unsupervised models), decision-tree surrogates for global explanation (Trustee, Metis, Mousika distillation), attention (DeepCASE), prototypes-by-design (LEXNet), logic-based attribution (VoTE-XAI). RECURRING MODELS BEING EXPLAINED: LSTM/GRU sequence models for alerts and flows, autoencoder/Kitsune-style anomaly detectors, RF/GBDT over flow features, CNNs over packet bytes (traffic classification), DRL controllers (Metis, EXPLORA). AUTHOR-STATED LIMITATIONS (the gap map): (1) Human evaluation is scarce and often bogus -- Nadeem SoK: user studies in 'only 14% of the cases' in security XAI; Nauta CSUR: '1 in 3 papers evaluate exclusively with anecdotal evidence, and 1 in 5 papers evaluate with users'; Buçinca: proxy tasks and subjective trust ratings do not predict real decision performance (so questionnaire-only SOC studies prove little); Kares: subjective and objective measures disagree. (2) When humans ARE tested, explanations often do not help or hurt: Poursabzi-Sangdeh: transparency 'hampered people's ability to detect when the model made a mistake, seemingly due to information overload'; Alqaraawi: saliency gave 'very limited help'; Sixt: simple baselines beat concept methods; van der Waa: explanations PERSUADE users to follow wrong advice; Zhang/Liao: 'trust calibration alone is not sufficient'; Fok & Weld: explanations only help when they enable verification, which alert triage rarely affords; Kaur: practitioners 'over-trust and misuse' SHAP/GAM tooling; Bhatt: deployed XAI serves ML engineers debugging, not end-user analysts. (3) SOC-specific asks: Alahmadi's analysts want alarms that are Reliable-Explainable-Analytical-Contextual-Transferable and complain most 'false positives' are benign triggers; Oesch found interface violations and mistrust of ML tools in situ; Nyre-Yu report integration/workflow friction as the dominant xAI barrier; Kokulu found manager-vs-analyst goal mismatches. (4) RUNTIME COST AT LINE RATE -- the sharpest under-studied edge: Warnecke et al. made efficiency an explicit criterion and found perturbation/black-box methods orders of magnitude slower than gradient methods (they report explanation runtimes, recommending white-box methods for security); exact Shapley is exponential, and even engineered versions are batch-oriented (GPUTreeShap ~1.2M rows/s on 8 V100s is impressive but that is a GPU cluster, not a switch ASIC); FastSHAP/amortized methods trade fidelity+training cost for single-forward-pass latency; TRUST XAI and VoTE-XAI both advertise speed vs LIME/SHAP for IIoT/5G monitoring; EXPLORA targets near-real-time RAN control loops; LEXNet and Mousika sidestep post-hoc cost entirely (explainable-by-design prototypes; distilled binary decision trees as ternary switch rules at line rate). NOBODY measures per-packet or per-flow explanation latency against actual line rates (1-100 Gbps) for traffic classification -- the field's runtime numbers are per-sample CPU/GPU seconds on desktop hardware; a paper quantifying the explanation-latency budget of an in-line NTC pipeline (and when amortized/by-design methods fit it) appears to be open. (5) Data/label realism: Teuwen shows SOC label imbalance corrupts explanation correctness itself; Apruzzese argues academic evaluations ignore practitioner-relevant costs (hardware, retraining, latency) and validates the complaint with a practitioner user study.
